title: Kingdom of Adiabene
capsule: The Kingdom of Adiabene was a semi-autonomous monarchy in northern Mesopotamia between the Upper and Lower Zab rivers, with its capital at Arbela (modern Erbil), that served as a vassal first of Parthia and later Sassanid Persia. Its royal family gained wide notoriety in the 1st century CE when Queen Helena and her son Izates II converted to Judaism; Helena subsequently moved to Jerusalem, sent grain to relieve a famine, and was buried there in a monument still visible in Roman-era accounts. Under Trajan's Parthian campaign of 115–116 CE Adiabene was briefly constituted as a Roman province, but Roman withdrawal restored Parthian suzerainty; Ardashir II is recorded as the last figure to bear the title of king of Adiabene around 379 CE.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The kingdom's general location is securely established by ancient sources including Josephus and Strabo, but precise territorial limits at any given date depend on fragmentary textual evidence and are not archaeologically mapped.
